speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In view of former Minister S Iswaran's court conviction, various Members in this House, including Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, have asked about the application of section 165 of the Penal Code and its impact on the wider Public Service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: My response today will also address the questions by Mr Yip Hon Weng1,2 and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim3, which are scheduled for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I invite Members to seek clarifications, if need be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the questions have been answered satisfactorily, it may not be necessary for Members to proceed with their Parliamentary Questions for future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We expect individuals in the Public Service to uphold high standards of conduct and this expectation extends to individuals carrying out functions on behalf of the Government, even if not directly employed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is important to preserve the integrity of our Public Service, so as to maintain public confidence and trust.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For an offence to be made out under section 165 of the Penal Code, the following conditions need to be met.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, section 165 applies only to public servants.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This generally includes public officers under the employment of the Public Service and various individuals executing public duties on behalf of the Government.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the public servant must have accepted or obtained a valuable thing for free or for inadequate payment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, the valuable thing must be accepted or obtained from a person whom the public servant personally knows to have been, or to be, or to be likely to be concerned in any business transaction connected to the public servant's official functions or where the business is transacted by the public servant in relation to his duties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In this context, a business transaction would commonly take the form of legal contract that is being negotiated or actively performed, applications for permits, licences and exemptions and ongoing investigations or assessments by Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With these as background, let me address some specific questions raised by Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, Ms Sylvia Lim asked if the definition of "public servant" under the Penal Code is fit for purpose for an offence under section 165 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Public servants carry out a wide range of functions on behalf of the Government.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The definition of "public servant" in the Penal Code is broad, so as to cover individuals who are entrusted with these public duties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I should also point out to Members of this House that being deemed as "public servants" under the Penal Code also offers the individuals protection when they are carrying out their public duties because there are specific provisions under the Penal Code that make offences more serious when committed against a public servant.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Section 332 of the Penal Code, voluntarily causing hurt to deter a public servant from his duty, is one example.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Under this provision, the offender will face a higher penalty than if he had committed the offence of voluntarily causing hurt against an ordinary member of the public, with all other things being equal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We expect high standards of conduct from all public servants.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Accepting or obtaining gifts from a person whom the public servant knows to be concerned in business transacted by that public servant or having a connection with that public servant's official functions is not acceptable in Singapore's context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Otherwise, public confidence in the impartiality and integrity of the Government would be undermined.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is also the ethos Singaporeans would expect of leaders in all organisations, whether private or public.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about the review of Chapter 9 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim have asked whether section 165 of the Penal Code may deter individuals and top talents from the private sector from joining or contributing to the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Individuals from the private sector who are serving as Chairpersons or Board Directors on our Statutory Boards play an important role in building resilient and effective public sector organisations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not think our rules would deter good people from joining our boards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the contrary, if we do not have an ethos or system that ensures clean, honest government, we would not be able to attract the right people from the private sector to join us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would also like to assure our Chairpersons and Board Directors that if they act professionally and with integrity, they have nothing to fear.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Sylvia Lim has asked about the impact of recent developments on public trust and whether our anti-corruption laws have to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However stringently we act against corruption, from time to time, individuals might fall short.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When this happens, we should not have a knee-jerk reaction and immediately tighten or add more rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, we ask ourselves whether it was an individual or systematic matter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the rules were unclear, we should clarify or simplify the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the rules were too lax or it was a new situation not envisaged or covered by the rules, we should update the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the individual level, we must have the right ethos and values, understand both the spirit and letter of the rules and uphold them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the team or organisation-level, we must look out for one another to minimise the chances of us being compromised, subverted or succumbing to human frailties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On my Question No 33 on the case itself, I have three questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Broadly, these questions surround my observation that the handling of this case has actually raised more questions than it has answered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And I would like to ask three specific questions to see if Minister will agree with me on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, would the public be justified to conclude that the corruption case against the former Minister was weak, hence, resulting in the reduction of charges, away from PCA?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second question is, because of the former Minister pleading guilty, there was no trial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, the evidence was not tested as such in the Court, but there was a plea bargain behind closed doors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister agree that such a way of handling the case under a plea bargain has now given rise to a lot of speculation in the public sphere as to what precisely happened on the facts and also between the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) and the Defence?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He, in fact, noted that what the Prosecution asked for was manifestly inadequate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have had residents come to me on this point to express their doubts as to whether the Public Prosecutor had defended the public interest adequately in this case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On Question No 33, part (b), on the PCA review, I do agree with the Minister that we should not have knee-jerk reactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, I was prompted to ask this question because it was the AGC's response when asked by the media on why the charges were reduced against the Minister, where they mentioned that there were litigation risks involved in proceeding against PCA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To quote them, what they said was, both the giver and the receiver of the gratification have a common interest to deny the corrupt element and, hence, it was risky to proceed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But does the Minister agree that actually this has not prevented prosecutions under the PCA in such scenarios, where both parties actually deny corruption?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And based on what the AGC has indicated, is this a reason for the Government to look again into PCA?
Ms Lim, as a lawyer, would know very well that it is not uncommon for charges to be amended on their way to the Courts because of developments or representations by the Prosecution and the defendant.
So, it is not odd because such things do happen regularly in the Courts.
The second part of the first comment is on sentencing.
We need to make a distinction between what the Prosecutor asked for and the Judge's discretion to mete out the sentence.
So, these two are quite separate and we should not conflate the two.
As of now, suffice to say that CPIB and our enforcement agencies find the current framing is able to allow us to do the job that we need to do.
But going forward, if there are new developments that necessitate us to do a review of this, we are open to that.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, how does the Ministry ensure that the public perception of incidents like the recent case does not inadvertently narrow the range of candidates willing to serve, particularly those who may have offered different perspectives due to a private sector background?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that many private sector professionals are accustomed a different business culture, how does the Ministry plan to ensure that the existing measures for navigating potential conflicts of interests are aligned with these cultural norms while at the same time maintaining public confidence?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, I will be very careful to not overplay the difference in the business culture and the Public Service culture when it comes to corruption.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are all Singaporeans and the international community knows that, in Singapore, we have clear rules and I would not want to suggest that somehow the private sector has a different set of rules or culture that is so different from the public sector.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second point, does this affect the public perception on whether good people will want to join us?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is precisely the point that I mentioned in my reply.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If our rules are not clear, if our execution of the rules are not clear and decisive, it will deter good people from wanting to join us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can see this in the experiences of other countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When rules are not clear or when rules are clear but enforcements are not done properly, it will actually deter good people from joining both the Public Service as employees and for serving the Public Service even if they are not employees, like, for example, being on our boards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, two further supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As he speaks on behalf of the Prime Minister, so these questions are actually directed at certain things the Prime Minister has said about the case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: When the former Minister was charged in January this year, Prime Minister Wong said, and I quote, "CPIB has done a thorough investigation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: They have dug deep and wide and they have presented their full investigations to the AGC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The AGC has decided to press charges against Mr Iswaran." So, nine months on, with the subsequent developments, I would like to ask whether it is still the Prime Minister's position that the CPIB and AGC did a thorough job in this case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second question, again, after the sentencing of the former Minister, the Prime Minister was quoted as saying that we need to act against corruption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But noting that the former Minister was not actually convicted of corruption, is the Prime Minister actually saying that regardless of the charges that were preferred and, finally, the former Minister was convicted on, he thinks that the former Minister acted corruptly?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It applies to the public officers, but it is a corruption charge.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second comment, do we have reasons to believe that CPIB and AGC did their job?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as I have mentioned and explained, along the way, it is not uncommon for the Prosecution and the Defence to see how the situation develops and, sometimes, charges may be amended in this situation or in any other cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: On the point of section 165, I believe it is the law that no corrupt element needs to be proved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That is why it is easier to get a conviction on section 165.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The difference between the PCA and section 165 is as follows: in section 165, you do not need to prove a quid pro quo on both sides.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You just need to prove that the person has taken.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It does not mean that it is not a corruption charge.
